questions.q: What is the most common (m/c) cause of primary hypothyroidism on page 905?
questions.exp: Under Primary Hypothyroidism: '1. Autoimmune hypothyroidism (m/c) AKA Hashimoto thyroiditis'. (Book p905)

questions.q: Autoimmune hypothyroidism is associated with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes (APS); clinicians should specifically check for ___ before initiating treatment.
questions.exp: Autoimmune hypothyroidism is associated with APS-1/2; clinicians 'Should check for APS2 before treatment'. (Book p905)

questions.q: A patient with undetected coexisting adrenal insufficiency (APS-2) is prescribed L-thyroxine without prior cortisol supplementation. What acute consequence is cautioned on page 905?
opts: Adrenal insufficiency: shock in children, profound adrenal insufficiency in adults
Sudden thyrotoxic crisis with hyperpyrexia and delirium
Acute hypocalcemic tetany from suppressed parathyroid reserve
questions.exp: If L-thyroxine is given without cortisol supplementation in APS-2, it precipitates adrenal insufficiency: shock in children, and profound adrenal insufficiency in adults. (Book p905)

questions.q: Match the pharmacologic agent causing hypothyroidism to its specific clinical characteristic — 1) Lithium 2) Interferon-alpha (IFN-α) 3) Amiodarone … A) Associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI) B) Drug-associated thyroid destruction (irreversible side effect) C) Can produce both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism
questions.exp: Lithium causes hypothyroidism and nephrogenic DI; IFN-α causes irreversible thyroid destruction; amiodarone can produce both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism. (Book p905)

questions.q: Regarding side effects of interferon-alpha (IFN-α): I Thyroid destruction is an irreversible side effect. II Flu-like syndrome is a reversible side effect.
opts: Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
questions.exp: Page 905 notes for IFN-α: 'Irreversible S/E: thyroid destruction' and 'Reversible S/E : Flu like syndrome'. (Book p905)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed under causes of primary hypothyroidism on page 905?
opts: Pituitary mass effect from lymphocytic hypophysitis
questions.exp: Pituitary mass effect is a cause of secondary hypothyroidism, not primary hypothyroidism. (Book p905)

questions.q: In secondary hypothyroidism due to a pituitary mass effect, what is the most common (m/c) underlying etiology listed?
questions.exp: Under Secondary Hypothyroidism: 'Pituitary cause : No significant hypothyroidism; Primary Cause - MASS effect - (m/c) Lymphocytic hypophysitis'. (Book p905)

questions.q: Assess secondary hypothyroidism from pituitary disease: I It characteristically causes severe, profound isolated hypothyroidism. II Its primary mechanism is mass effect, most commonly from lymphocytic hypophysitis.
opts: I is true; II is false
Both I and II are false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are true
questions.exp: Page 905 states: 'No significant hypothyroidism' for pituitary cause, and its primary cause is mass effect, most commonly lymphocytic hypophysitis. (Book p905)

questions.q: A 2-month-old infant with a large hepatic hemangioma develops profound hypothyroidism requiring massive doses of levothyroxine. What is the mechanism of this consumptive hypothyroidism?
opts: Suppression of hypothalamic TRH secretion by circulating angiogenin
Increased deiodinase-III expression in the hemangioma converting active hormone to reverse T3
Direct destruction of the infant thyroid follicles by hemangioma-derived antibodies
Failure of intestinal absorption of thyroid hormone due to splanchnic steal
questions.exp: Consumptive hypothyroidism in hemangioma is driven by increased deiodinase-III expression leading to decreased active hormones and increased reverse T3. (Book p905)

questions.q: Consumptive hypothyroidism associated with hemangioma is mediated by increased expression of ___, which accelerates the formation of ___.
questions.exp: Hemangioma -> ↑ Deiodinase-III expression -> ↓ Hormones (↑ formation of Reverse T3). (Book p905)

questions.q: What is the primary underlying cause of congenital hypothyroidism on page 905?
questions.exp: Under Congenital Hypothyroidism: 'mostly due to thyroid dysgenesis'. (Book p905)

questions.q: Match the newborn physical sign of congenital hypothyroidism to its system — 1) Cranial sign 2) Gastrointestinal sign 3) Hepatic sign … A) Open posterior fontanelle B) Delay in passing meconium C) Prolonged physiological jaundice
questions.exp: Features of congenital hypothyroidism listed on page 905 are: open posterior fontanelle, delay in passing meconium, and prolonged physiological jaundice. (Book p905)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed on page 905 as a feature of congenital hypothyroidism?
opts: Delay in passing meconium and prolonged physiological jaundice
Very little crying and excessive sleep
questions.exp: Features of congenital hypothyroidism are open posterior fontanelle, delay in passing meconium, prolonged physiological jaundice, very little crying, and excessive sleep. (Book p905)

questions.q: In which demographic group is Hashimoto's thyroiditis most common?
questions.exp: Under Hashimoto's Thyroiditis FEATURES: 'most common in middle-aged female'. (Book p906)

questions.q: Match the immunogenetic associations of Hashimoto's thyroiditis — 1) HLA alleles 2) Immune checkpoint polymorphisms … A) HLA-DR3, DR4, DR5 (can be ANA positive) B) CTLA-4 and PTPN-22 polymorphisms
questions.exp: HLA associations are DR-3 / DR-4 / DR5 (can be ANA +ve); non-HLA gene polymorphisms are CTLA-4 / PTPN-22. (Book p906)

questions.q: Assess gland changes in Hashimoto's thyroiditis: I The thyroid gland is commonly not enlarged. II When goitre is present, it is characteristically an irregular, firm, heterogeneous, non-tender enlargement.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
questions.exp: Gland changes: 'Commonly not enlarged' and 'If goitre present : Irregular/ firm/ heterogeneous non tender enlargement of gland'. (Book p906)

questions.q: On gross examination of a resected thyroid from a middle-aged woman with autoimmune hypothyroidism, the gland appears fibrosed, pale, and firm. What accounts for the pale appearance?
opts: Diffuse fatty infiltration of stromal tissue
questions.exp: Under Gross appearance: 'Fibrosed gland' and 'Pale gland d/t lymphoid infiltration'. (Book p906)

questions.q: On microscopic examination of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, the prominent lymphocytic infiltration characteristically organizes into ___ formation.
questions.exp: Microscopic appearance: 'Lymphocytic infiltration -> Germinal center formation'. (Book p906)

questions.q: What are the transformed, hypereosinophilic epithelial cells with abundant granular cytoplasm seen in Hashimoto's thyroiditis called?
questions.exp: Page 906 notes: 'Hypereosinophilic cells : Hürthle cells' and 'Oxyphilic metaplasia'. (Book p906)

questions.q: Regarding the microscopic findings in Hashimoto's thyroiditis: I The follicular lumen characteristically shows an absence of colloid. II Oxyphilic metaplasia with Hürthle cells is a key hallmark.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
questions.exp: Microscopic hallmarks on page 906 include: 'Absence of colloid' and 'Oxyphilic metaplasia' with Hürthle cells. (Book p906)

questions.q: Which malignancy has the highest associated relative risk in patients with longstanding Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
opts: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid
questions.exp: Under Associated malignancy: 'Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid'. (Book p906)

questions.q: Match the malignancy associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis to its relative frequency order — 1) Most strongly associated malignancy 2) Secondary associated thyroid carcinoma … A) Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma B) Papillary carcinoma thyroid
questions.exp: Associated malignancy hierarchy: Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma is more strongly associated than papillary carcinoma of thyroid. (Book p906)

questions.q: The cellular and cytokine mediators driving thyroid destruction in Hashimoto's include T-cells (both CD-8 and ___), plasma cells, and the cytokine ___.
questions.exp: Pathological mediators: 'T-cell (CD-8, CD-4)', 'IFN-gamma', and 'Plasma cell'. (Book p906)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed on page 906 as a histological feature or mediator of Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
opts: Lymphocytic infiltration with germinal center formation
Abundant colloid retention in dilated follicles
questions.exp: In Hashimoto's, there is characteristically an 'Absence of colloid', not abundant colloid retention. (Book p906)

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with a 15-year history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis presents with a rapidly enlarging thyroid goiter. Biopsy demonstrates extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma. What is the classic risk hierarchy noted on page 906?
opts: Follicular thyroid carcinoma > marginal zone lymphoma
Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid
Papillary carcinoma thyroid > follicular carcinoma thyroid
Medullary thyroid carcinoma > anaplastic thyroid carcinoma
questions.exp: Page 906 explicitly highlights: 'Associated malignancy : Extranodal marginal zone lymphoma > papillary carcinoma thyroid'. (Book p906)

questions.q: What is the most common (m/c) presenting symptom of generalized slowing (decreased BMR) in primary and secondary hypothyroidism?
questions.exp: Under Classical Symptoms: '1. Generalized slowing (↓ BMR) : Fatigue/tiredness (m/c)'. (Book p907)

questions.q: Match the manifestations of generalized slowing in hypothyroidism — 1) Speech & Gait 2) Bowel movements 3) Neurologic reflexes 4) Body weight … A) Slow speech and slow gait B) Constipation C) Delayed deep tendon reflexes (DTR) D) Poor appetite with weight gain
questions.exp: Generalized slowing affects: speech/gait (slow), bowel (constipation), reflexes (delayed DTR), and weight (poor appetite with weight gain). (Book p907)

questions.q: In primary hypothyroidism, elevated TSH stimulates fibroblasts to produce matrix ___, which trap water and cause non-pitting myxedema.
questions.exp: In 1° Hypothyroidism: ↑ TSH elevation -> Stimulates Fibroblast -> Stimulates Accumulation of matrix GAG's -> Traps water -> Nonpitting edema. (Book p907)

questions.q: Assess the clinical consequences of matrix GAG accumulation trapping water in 1° hypothyroidism: I Facial puffiness, periorbital edema, and hoarse voice. II Macroglossia leading to obstructive sleep apnea syndrome.
opts: Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
questions.exp: Trapped water from matrix GAGs causes puffiness (face), periorbital edema, macroglossia -> obstructive sleep apnea syndrome, hoarse voice, and nonpitting edema. (Book p907)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed on page 907 as a symptom predominant in young females with hypothyroidism?
questions.exp: Symptoms predominant in young females are hair loss, irregular menstrual cycle, dry skin, and mood swings. (Book p907)

questions.q: Which endocrine disorder is noted on page 907 as causing 'False positive Hypothyroidism' (transiently elevated TSH)?
questions.exp: Page 907 explicitly contains the note: 'Note : False positive Hypothyroidism -> Addison's disease'. (Book p907)

questions.q: An adult with severe longstanding primary hypothyroidism presents with prominent pseudohypertrophy of both calf muscles accompanied by slowness and muscle stiffness. What eponymous disorder is depicted in the photo on page 907?
questions.exp: The clinical photo on page 907 demonstrates: 'Hoffman syndrome Pseudohypertrophy in calf muscle'. (Book p907)

questions.q: Match the serous cavity effusions seen in hypothyroid polyserositis — 1) Pleural cavity 2) Pericardial space 3) Peritoneal cavity … A) Pleural effusion B) Pericardial effusion C) Ascites
questions.exp: Complications of hypothyroidism include serous effusions in three spaces: pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, and ascites. (Book p907)

questions.q: What is the most common cause of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) in females versus males on page 907?
questions.exp: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS): 'm/c cause in females : Hypothyroidism' and 'm/c cause in males : Amyloidosis'. (Book p907)

questions.q: Regarding Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) epidemiology on page 907: I Hypothyroidism is the most common cause in females. II Amyloidosis is the most common cause in males.
opts: Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
I is false; II is true
questions.exp: Page 907 notes for CTS: - m/c cause in females : Hypothyroidism, - m/c cause in males : Amyloidosis. (Book p907)

questions.q: A 48-year-old obese woman with untreated hypothyroidism presents with severe loud snoring, daytime sleepiness, and witnessed nocturnal apneas. What anatomical mechanism links this to her thyroid disease?
opts: Macroglossia secondary to TSH-induced matrix GAG accumulation causing obstructive sleep apnea syndrome
Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve compression from thyroid fibrosis
Direct neuromuscular weakness of the diaphragm from hypothyroid myopathy
Tracheal deviation from subacute granulomatous expansion
questions.exp: GAG accumulation traps water, producing macroglossia that leads directly to obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. (Book p907)

questions.q: Although page 907 prints 'Hypocholesterolaemia' among complications (an editorial misprint in the scan), the classical metabolic consequence of reduced LDL clearance in hypothyroidism is ___.
questions.exp: Page 907 lists 'Hypocholesterolemia' in its complications column, but clinically and on page 903, impaired cholesterol clearance classically causes hypercholesterolemia. (Book p907)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed on page 907 as a complication of hypothyroidism?
opts: Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome and Carpal tunnel syndrome
questions.exp: Hypercalcemia and nephrolithiasis are complications of severe thyrotoxicosis (p903), not hypothyroidism. Complications on p907 are myxedema coma, encephalopathy, bradycardia, effusions, OSA, and CTS. (Book p907)

questions.q: In a patient presenting with newly identified hypothyroidism, autoantibody screening returns completely negative. What diagnostic entity is considered on page 908?
opts: Transient hypothyroidism due to thyroiditis (postviral or post-vaccine)
questions.exp: In the workup for Hashimoto's, negative autoantibodies indicate: 'Transient Hypothyroidism : Thyroiditis (Postviral / Post vaccine) -> may/may not require treatment'. (Book p908)

questions.q: Match the autoantibody in Hashimoto's disease to its percentage association on page 908 — 1) Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibody 2) Thyroglobulin antibody 3) TSH Receptor Antibody … A) 90 - 100% B) 80 - 90% C) 10 - 20%
questions.exp: Autoantibody associations in Hashimoto's: TPO Ab 90 - 100%, Thyroglobulin Ab 80 - 90%, and TSH Receptor Ab 10 - 20%. (Book p908)

questions.q: The single most sensitive and prevalent autoantibody in Hashimoto's disease is ___, present in ___ of cases.
questions.exp: Thyroid peroxidase antibody is the most strongly associated antibody, present in 90 - 100% of Hashimoto's patients. (Book p908)

questions.q: Match the combination of elevated TSH (↑ TSH) and free T4 level to the diagnosis — 1) ↓ Free T4 2) ↑ Free T4 3) Normal Free T4 … A) 1° Hypothyroidism B) TSH Secreting Adenoma C) Subclinical 1° Hypothyroidism
questions.exp: ↑ TSH + ↓ Free T4 = 1° Hypothyroidism; ↑ TSH + ↑ Free T4 = TSH Secreting Adenoma; ↑ TSH + Normal Free T4 = Subclinical 1° Hypothyroidism. (Book p908)

questions.q: What is the definitive TSH cut-off value that provides an absolute indication for L-thyroxine treatment in confirmed Hashimoto's disease regardless of symptoms?
questions.exp: Under Treatment Indications: 'Confirmed Hashimoto's (TSH value > 10 mcu/ltr)'. (Book p908)

questions.q: For patients with a TSH value between 5 and 10 mcu/ltr: I Treatment is indicated if vague symptoms are present with TPO positivity, positive family history, or pregnancy. II Treatment is indicated if severe symptoms are present.
opts: I is false; II is true
Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true; II is false
questions.exp: When TSH is 5 - 10 mcu/ltr, treatment is indicated for vague symptoms + (TPO +ve, Family history, Pregnancy) or severe symptoms. (Book p908)

questions.q: A 27-year-old woman in early pregnancy is found to have a TSH of 6.8 mcu/ltr with normal free T4. Her anti-TPO antibody titre is elevated. What is the correct management per page 908?
opts: Defer treatment and recheck TSH postpartum
Wait until TSH exceeds 10 mcu/ltr before treating
questions.exp: In pregnancy with TSH 5 - 10 mcu/ltr and TPO positivity, L-thyroxine treatment is explicitly indicated. (Book p908)

questions.q: What is the recommended starting dose of L-thyroxine for a symptomatic hypothyroid patient under 60 years of age?
questions.exp: For < 60 yr + symptomatic: 'L-Thyroxine 1.6-1.8 µg/kg/day (Approx 100µg/day)'. (Book p908)

questions.q: In patients under 60 years of age on L-thyroxine, subsequent dosage adjustments should be titrated by ___ µg/day.
questions.exp: Under drugs: 'Dose change can be by 25-50 µg/day' for patients under 60 years. (Book p908)

questions.q: In elderly patients (> 60 years of age), what is the recommended starting dose and dose adjustment step for L-thyroxine?
opts: Starting dose 50 µg/day; dose change by 50 µg/day
Starting dose 100 µg/day; dose change by 25 µg/day
Starting dose 10 µg/day; dose change by 5 µg/day
Starting dose 25 µg/day; dose change by 25 µg/day
questions.exp: In elderly (>60 yr): starting dose is '25 µg/day' and 'Dose change by 25 µg/day'. (Book p908)

questions.q: Why must elderly patients (> 60 years) be started on a low dose of L-thyroxine (25 µg/day)?
opts: Because older patients do not convert T4 to T3
Due to the risk of cardiotoxicity (e.g., precipitating angina or arrhythmias)
Because of rapid hepatic clearance of levothyroxine in older adults
Due to the high risk of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
questions.exp: Elderly patients start at 25 µg/day explicitly '(Due to cardiotoxicity)'. (Book p908)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an indication to treat subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH 5 - 10 mcu/ltr on page 908?
opts: Vague symptoms with a positive family history
Pregnancy or presence of severe symptoms
questions.exp: Indications for TSH 5-10 mcu/ltr are: vague symptoms + TPO +ve, family history, pregnancy, or severe symptoms. (Book p908)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: What specific administration instructions must be given to patients taking oral L-thyroxine on page 909?
opts: Take dissolved in hot milk twice daily after meals
Take on an empty stomach in the morning (7 - 7:30 am) with a glass of water, and wait 30 minutes before meals
Take with a full meal at dinner time to maximize lipid-phase absorption
Take at bedtime co-administered with calcium and iron supplements
questions.exp: Instructions: 'Empty stomach (morning 7-7:30 am) with glass of water. Take meal after 30 minutes'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: Match the drug that inhibits L-thyroxine absorption to its formulation — 1) FeSO4 2) CaCO3 3) Al(OH)3 / Sucralfate … A) Ferrous sulfate iron salt B) Calcium carbonate C) Aluminum hydroxide antacid / mucosal protectant
questions.exp: Drugs to be avoided because they inhibit absorption include FeSO4, CaCO3, Al(OH)3, and Sucralfate. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: The single most common (m/c) cause of treatment failure in hypothyroid patients prescribed L-thyroxine is ___.
questions.exp: Under follow-up: 'm/c cause of treatment failure : Non-compliance'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: How long after the serum TSH value normalizes does the patient typically achieve clinical symptomatic relief?
questions.exp: Page 909 explicitly notes: 'Clinical relief : 3-6 months after TSH value becomes normal'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: What is the mortality rate of myxedema coma reported on page 909?
questions.exp: Under Emergency Conditions: 'myxedema coma : mortality 40%'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: What are the primary trigger factors listed for precipitating myxedema coma?
opts: Non-compliance and infection (e.g., COVID-19 or lower respiratory tract infection - LRI)
Excessive dietary iodine and strenuous physical exertion
questions.exp: Trigger factors for myxedema coma: 'Non-compliance, infection (i.e. covid, LRI)'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: Match the characteristic 'Hypo' presenting features of myxedema coma — 1) Respiratory 2) Glucose metabolism 3) Electrolytes 4) Body temperature … A) Hypoventilation B) Hypoglycemia C) Hyponatremia D) Hypothermia
questions.exp: The 'Hypo' tetrad of myxedema coma consists of Hypoventilation, Hypoglycemia, Hyponatremia, and Hypothermia. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: An elderly woman with myxedema coma is admitted with severe bradycardia, hypothermia (34°C), and low-voltage ECG complexes. Which intravenous fluid is indicated, and which must be avoided?
opts: Hypotonic saline indicated; hypertonic saline strictly avoided
5% Dextrose in water indicated; hypertonic saline strictly avoided
Albumin colloid indicated; normal saline strictly avoided
Hypertonic saline indicated; hypotonic saline strictly avoided
questions.exp: Treatment specifies: 'Hypertonic saline (Avoid hypotonic saline)'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: What is the complete medical treatment regimen for myxedema coma on page 909?
opts: IV Levothyroxine 25 µg daily, Furosemide infusion, Potassium chloride
IV L-thyroxine 500 µg OD -> 50-100 µg/day, Steroid, IV T3 5-20 µg, Hypertonic saline
Oral PTU 1000 mg stat, Propranolol 60 mg Q4H, Iopanoic acid, Normal saline
External active warming with heated blankets, Hydrocortisone, Hypotonic saline
questions.exp: Treatment for myxedema coma: IV L-thyroxine 500 µg OD -> 50-100 µg/day, Steroid, IV T3 5-20 µg, and Hypertonic saline. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroid illness (SREAT / Hashimoto encephalopathy) is an autoimmune vasculitis that is ___ to thyroid function, and can be seen in ___ status.
questions.exp: SREAT: 'Can be seen in euthyroid status' and is an 'Autoimmune vasculitis unrelated to thyroid function'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: Which autoantibody and HLA allele are characteristically elevated and associated with SREAT on page 909?
questions.exp: SREAT is characterized by '↑↑ Antibodies (Anti-enolase Ab)' and 'HLA -B8'. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: Match the clinical presentations of SREAT — 1) Progressive cognitive decline 2) Paroxysmal motor events 3) Vascular mimic … A) Altered level of consciousness B) Seizure & myoclonus C) Stroke-like presentation
questions.exp: Presentations of SREAT include: slowly progressive cognitive decline (altered level of consciousness), seizure & myoclonus, and stroke-like presentation. (Book p909)

questions.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy
questions.q: Assess SREAT management on page 909: I The primary and definitive pharmacologic management is corticosteroids (steroids). II Patients must immediately receive high-dose intravenous levothyroxine.
opts: Both I and II are false
I is true; II is false
Both I and II are true
I is false; II is true
questions.exp: Management of SREAT is explicitly stated as 'management : Steroids'. Thyroid hormone therapy is not the primary treatment since SREAT is vasculitic and unrelated to thyroid function. (Book p909)

units.title: Hypothyroidism Classification & Causes
units.sec: Primary, Secondary, Consumptive & Congenital Hypothyroidism · p905
units.guide: Master primary causes (Hashimoto, APS-2 check prior to L-thyroxine, drugs including lithium, IFN-α, and amiodarone), secondary causes (lymphocytic hypophysitis mass effect), consumptive hypothyroidism (hemangioma D3 overexpression), and newborn congenital signs.

units.title: Hashimoto's Thyroiditis Features, Pathology & Mediators
units.sec: Hashimoto Features, Histology & Associated Malignancy · p906
units.guide: Cover demographics (middle-aged females), HLA associations (DR3/DR4/DR5, CTLA-4, PTPN-22), gross and microscopic features (Hürthle cells, lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, absence of colloid), extranodal marginal zone lymphoma risk, and immune mediators (CD8/CD4 T-cells, IFN-γ).

units.title: Clinical Presentation, Signs & Complications of Hypothyroidism
units.sec: Symptoms, Signs, GAG Deposition & Complications · p907
units.guide: Examine generalized slowing, TSH-stimulated GAG deposition causing myxedema (periorbital edema, macroglossia, OSA), young female symptoms, false-positive Addison's, Hoffman syndrome, polyserositis, and carpal tunnel syndrome.

units.title: Hashimoto Workup, Diagnostic Cut-offs & L-Thyroxine Dosing
units.sec: Autoantibodies, Treatment Indications & L-Thyroxine Titration · p908
units.guide: Work through autoantibody prevalence (TPO 90-100%, Tg 80-90%, TSH-R 10-20%), subclinical vs overt cut-offs, treatment threshold (TSH > 10 or 5-10 with risks), starting doses (< 60 yrs 1.6-1.8 µg/kg/day vs elderly 25 µg/day), and titration increments.

units.title: L-Thyroxine Administration, Follow-up, Myxedema Coma & SREAT
units.sec: Patient Instructions, Myxedema Coma & SREAT / Hashimoto Encephalopathy · p909
units.guide: Review morning empty-stomach dosing, drugs to avoid, 3-month review, myxedema coma presentation (hypothermia, low voltage ECG) and IV protocol, and SREAT (euthyroid vasculitis, anti-enolase antibodies, steroid response).
